title: Efficient ≠ Good
author: Paul Kirschner
summary: Paul Kirschner pushes back on the recurring claim that Generative AI will 'transform' education, arguing that producing text quickly is not the same as teaching well and saving teacher time is not the same as improving student learning. He grounds the critique in a real randomized controlled trial by Sungu, Lira, and Duckworth ('Generative AI Can Harm Teaching') conducted across fourteen Turkish middle and secondary schools, involving 193 teachers and over 2,800 students — a large, real-world study rather than a lab or self-report survey. The headline finding: students whose teachers had access to a GPT-4o-based tool reported lower intrinsic motivation and found their courses less enjoyable and interesting. Kirschner uses this evidence to reinforce his long-standing cognitive-load-theory argument that efficiency is not synonymous with instructional quality or learning gains, cautioning educators against adopting GenAI tools on the promise of efficiency alone.

quotes: We're now being told, usually with great confidence and little to no evidence, that Generative AI (GenAI) will 'transform' education.
The problem is that producing text quickly isn't the same as teaching well, and saving teacher time isn't the same as improving student learning.
A randomised field experiment by Alp Sungu, Benjamin Lira, and Angela Duckworth (Generative AI Can Harm Teaching) provides a much needed reality check.
The analysis covered 193 teachers, 2,816 students and more than 14,000 student-course observations; not bad for a RCT in a real school under real learning conditions.
this wasn't a self-report survey nor a lab study using an artificial task. It examined what happened when teachers used GenAI in real schools.
